title: Autonomous Field Rover & Sensor Platform
summary: A modular Raspberry Pi/Linux field robotics platform for geotagged sensing, remote diagnostics, computer-vision development, and future autonomous operation.
overview: I am developing a modular field robotics platform for sensor integration, field-data collection, computer-vision development, and future autonomous operation. The current prototype is intentionally human-powered so the sensing, electrical, software, and safety systems can be validated before powered mobility is introduced.

The platform is designed as a reusable robotics system rather than around one demo. Current work emphasizes reliable field data, repeatable diagnostics, and architecture that can migrate to a larger powered rover.
objectives: Make field data repeatable enough to support later computer-vision and autonomy work.
Expose faults and sensor-health problems early instead of discovering them after a field run.
Keep the electrical/software interfaces modular enough to migrate onto a larger powered rover.
Validate sensing and safety before introducing propulsion as another source of failure.
role: Linux service design and onboard software integration
Remote diagnostics, networking, and health monitoring
process: Separated high-bandwidth sensing from embedded control so each side could evolve without forcing wholesale rewrites.
Built capture and monitoring as services with stable device mapping, health checks, diagnostics, and remote access.
Structured field capture around raw imagery, sensor data, timing, diagnostics, and location metadata rather than one-off demos.
Kept the prototype human-powered until sensing, safety, and observability were reliable enough to justify adding propulsion.
results: Onboard Linux computing, remote access, and camera capture are operational.
Stable device mapping, system-health monitoring, and diagnostics are working on the prototype.
Safety-state logic and structured field-data capture are implemented.
Localization and remaining sensor integration are the current validation focus before powered mobility.
evidence: Show sensing, compute, communications, safety, and logging together.
Establish the physical system and current prototype state.
Prove remote observability and repeatable capture tooling.

title: UBCO Aerospace — 2026 Urban Firefighting Drone System
summary: Electrical-system leadership for a multi-drone autonomous firefighting project that placed 6th overall and won the 2026 AEAC Innovation Award.
overview: From January 2025 to June 2026, I served as Director of Electrical for the UBCO Aerospace Team. The 2026 competition mission was urban firefighting; the rules did not require a multi-aircraft solution.

Our team deliberately pursued a mothership architecture instead of the more conventional single-aircraft approach. That architectural choice became the defining innovation of the system and was recognized with the 2026 AEAC Innovation Award.
objectives: Create an electrical system that could support the team's mothership concept without making integration fragile.
Give autonomy and sensing teams dependable power, data interfaces, and fault boundaries.
Reduce electrical mass and integration risk while keeping the aircraft practical to assemble, test, and troubleshoot.
Make cross-team interfaces explicit enough that electrical, mechanical, autonomy, and software work could progress in parallel.
role: Directed the electrical subteam and owned the top-level electrical architecture.
Defined electrical interfaces with autonomy, software, sensing, communications, and mechanical subsystems.
Led design reviews, work breakdown, milestone planning, and integration readiness.
Designed and integrated key power-distribution, sensing, and communications hardware.
process: Mapped power, data, sensing, and communications interfaces around the mothership concept before committing to detailed hardware.
Integrated LiDAR, RTK GNSS, IMU, cameras, LTE, Ethernet, and CAN around the flight/autonomy compute.
Designed the protected distribution architecture and a custom 50 V to 5 V, 40 W synchronous converter that reached approximately 92% efficiency.
Used peer review, milestone gates, and subsystem readiness checks to reduce late electrical/software/mechanical conflicts.
results: The mothership architecture received the 2026 AEAC Innovation Award.
The team placed 6th overall at the 2026 AEAC competition.
The completed system integrated sensing, communications, power, and autonomy hardware into a competition-ready aircraft architecture.
The development process provided a repeatable interface and review structure for multidisciplinary integration.

title: Mountain Resort Data Collection System — UBC Capstone
summary: A low-power distributed sensing system using ESP32 edge nodes, LoRa networking, ToF/mmWave sensing, custom power electronics, and a Linux gateway.
overview: My UBC capstone team developed a distributed data-collection system intended for harsh mountain-resort deployment. Edge sensing nodes communicated over LoRa to a Linux gateway, spanning power electronics, sensing, wireless networking, enclosure constraints, and system-level validation.
objectives: Operate remote sensing nodes under limited energy and harsh environmental constraints.
Move data reliably over long-range wireless links.

Designed the custom PCB schematic/layout and supported assembly and bench validation.
Selected batteries and electrical components against the deployment constraints.
Researched LoRa and sensing options and documented the resulting design decisions.
process: Used ESP32 edge nodes and a Linux gateway so sensing could remain distributed while analysis/visualization stayed centralized.
Implemented power conversion, battery monitoring, and low-voltage protection on the custom node hardware.
Evaluated batteries, energy demand, enclosure needs, sensing options, and Canadian 915 MHz requirements together rather than independently.
Bench-tested the electronics, then validated communication and the complete sensor-to-dashboard data path.
results: Demonstrated more than 500 m outdoor LoRa communication.
Demonstrated end-to-end sensing-to-dashboard data flow.

title: “Chimera” FPV Drone Frame
summary: A crash-driven custom FPV frame redesign focused on center-of-mass placement, crash behavior, packaging, and lightweight manufacture.
overview: After an FPV crash broke an arm on an existing frame, I used the failure as the starting point for a redesign around component packaging, center-of-mass placement, crash behavior, repairability, and a smaller footprint.

The project was less about producing a visually different frame and more about changing how the aircraft handled failure. The design explored intentional mechanical failure points so crash behavior could be more predictable instead of allowing damage to propagate arbitrarily through the assembly.
objectives: Use the previous crash to decide what should fail, what should survive, and what should be easy to replace.
Improve mass distribution and component packaging without growing the frame.
Prototype structural and packaging changes cheaply before committing to carbon fiber and aluminum.
role: Owned the frame geometry and component packaging.
Ran the rapid-prototyping loop from CAD through printed fit checks.
Prepared the design for final carbon-fiber/aluminum manufacture.
Integrated the electronics into the revised packaging.
process: Treated the broken arm as a load-path and serviceability problem rather than simply reproducing the old geometry.
Repositioned the battery and electronics while tightening the footprint and improving mass distribution.
Explored intentional sacrificial features so future crash energy would be more likely to damage replaceable parts instead of propagating unpredictably.
Used printed prototypes to verify fit and geometry before moving to the final carbon-fiber/aluminum parts.
results: Completed the final frame in 2024.
Continued flight/crash testing informed future modification ideas.
evidence: Show final geometry and component packaging.

title: Axial Flux Brushless DC Motor
summary: A custom axial-flux BLDC motor and geared scissor mechanism built with custom coils, 3D-printed structure, and iterative troubleshooting.
overview: This university project developed a custom axial-flux BLDC motor and geared scissor-cutting mechanism using 3D-printed mechanical parts, custom-wound coils, and existing drone hardware.

The axial configuration was chosen instead of defaulting to a conventional radial layout. Its layered construction made the motor easier to reason about as separate rotor, air-gap, stator/coil, and structural interfaces, so parallel iterations could be made without forcing a complete redesign every time one layer changed.
objectives: Demonstrate a functional custom motor rather than optimize a textbook geometry.
Use the axial layout to keep rotor, winding, air-gap, and structure changes as independent as practical.
Prove the motor against a real mechanical load and use failure as design feedback.
role: Mechanical/CAD design of the motor assembly
Coil geometry, winding, and electrical integration
process: Selected an axial-flux configuration so rotor, coil/stator, spacing, and structure could be iterated as distinct layers around stable interfaces.
Designed six coils in a wye configuration while balancing magnetic air gap, structural rigidity, packaging, and manufacturability.
3D printed the structure, wound and wired the coils, assembled the motor, and integrated the geared scissor mechanism.
The motor ran under mechanical load; PLA thermal deformation and rotor stability exposed the main limits of the first structural implementation.
results: Successfully ran the custom motor and drove the geared scissor mechanism.
Physical testing exposed PLA thermal deformation and rotor-stability limits that would drive the next structural revision.
Received a documented project grade of 100%.
evidence: Show the motor doing mechanical work.
Turn the V1 limitation into an iteration story.

title: Custom Upgraded 3D Printer
summary: A heavily modified Ender 3 Pro focused on print quality, material capability, maintainability, thermal management, wiring, and stability.
overview: I progressively rebuilt a Creality Ender 3 Pro around print quality, expanded material capability, electrical safety, serviceability, and mechanical stability.
objectives: Extend the machine's useful material/process range.
Improve service access and electrical organization instead of accumulating ad-hoc modifications.
Address Z-axis alignment, structural stability, and calibration as coupled problems.
role: Planned and executed the electrical/mechanical retrofit sequence.
Completed wiring, crimping, soldering, and electronics packaging.
Modified firmware and recalibrated the machine after hardware changes.
process: Assembled and calibrated the stock machine so later changes could be compared against a known configuration.
Reworked the control/electronics package with upgraded hardware, connectors, wiring, and cooling.
Added bracing, dual-Z drive, and a custom alignment mechanism to address stability and geometry.
Recalibrated firmware and slicer settings only after the revised hardware was mechanically and electrically stable.
results: Rebuilt the electronics package with upgraded controls, connectors, wiring, and cooling for easier access and service.
Added a second Z leadscrew, structural bracing, and a custom alignment mechanism to address mechanical stability and alignment.
Retuned firmware and slicer settings after the hardware changes and completed the final upgraded machine with broader material/process capability.

title: Guitar Filter & Compressor
summary: A MATLAB frequency-domain audio project that isolates chord tones and normalizes their amplitudes with band-pass filtering and compression.
overview: This individual project used MATLAB to process an acoustic-guitar chord in the frequency domain, isolate notes, and normalize their amplitudes.
objectives: Apply Fourier/filter concepts to audio.
Equalize tone amplitudes.
Generalize beyond the fixed assignment input.
process: Used the Fourier domain to identify the chord's dominant tone regions.
Built band-pass filters around the target notes rather than altering the entire spectrum uniformly.
Scaled isolated components toward a common amplitude before reconstruction.
Extended the script beyond the original fixed input so audio/chord frequencies could be user-selected.
results: Reduced final tone-amplitude variance to 1.2%.
Received a documented grade of 98%.
